Sources.Title: In the Zone: Manchester City 3–0 Bayern
Sources.Observation: City added a midfielder from the back line to build with two central links behind its front five.

Sources.Title: In the Zone: Manchester City 1–0 Inter
Sources.Observation: Inter disrupted the pivot and stepping defenders opened spaces behind them. City found a goal through a delayed midfield arrival and a cutback.

Sources.Title: The importance of in-game management
Sources.Context: Manchester City–Real Madrid, 2024 Champions League quarter-final
Sources.Observation: City moved the ball across a back three to draw a striker from Madrid’s 4-4-2 and create space for a central receiver.

Sources.Title: Europa League final: How Antonio Conte upgraded Inter
Sources.Observation: The three-centre-back structure supported advanced wing-backs, a holding midfielder, and forwards with complementary strengths.

Sources.Title: Match analysis: Roma 0–2 Leverkusen
Sources.Observation: The deep midfield pair found central passing lanes. Wing-backs changed lanes and attacked gaps created by the striker and attacking midfielders.

Sources.Title: Technical reports: 2023/24 club competitions
Sources.Observation: Atalanta denied Leverkusen’s build-up options with aggressive player-to-player pressure. The approach depended on defenders capable of handling isolated duels.

Sources.Title: In the Zone: Benfica 1–3 Liverpool
Sources.Observation: A compact counter-press and a high line helped Liverpool recover possession. The centre-backs needed to protect substantial space behind them.

Sources.Title: 2015/16 Europa League technical report
Sources.Coach: Jürgen Klopp; Unai Emery; Sir Alex Ferguson (technical observer)
Sources.Context: Liverpool–Sevilla final and sustainability of pressing
Sources.Observation: Liverpool’s early pressure in the final became harder to sustain. UEFA’s observers examined the spacing and physical demands that followed.

Sources.Title: Arsenal’s aggressive pressing against Paris
Sources.Observation: Arsenal pressed as a unit from a compact block, directing play towards one flank. The line behind the first press supported the move.

Sources.Title: Controlling the game without the ball
Sources.Observation: A connected mid-block can close central lanes while conceding some width. Counter-attacks become available as the attacking side commits more players.

Sources.Title: Group-stage review: Counter-pressing and goalkeeper distribution
Sources.Observation: Short collective pressing distances and cover behind the press helped teams contain transitions. FIFA highlighted the use of three defenders with two players screening ahead.

Sources.Title: France: Rest attack and counter-attacking efficiency
Sources.Observation: France kept an advanced outlet available before winning the ball. The position of that outlet shaped the first pass after the regain.

Sources.Title: Wing play with Aidy Boothroyd
Sources.Observation: Wide progression depends on supporting movements and timing as well as the ability of the player providing width.

Sources.Title: How to coach transition
Sources.Observation: The first presser or runner needs support. A defender can adjust to cover a full-back who advances.

Sources.Title: How to defend like England: transition
Sources.Observation: Recovering defenders protect the central space and delay the attack until teammates can recover.

Sources.Title: 2022/23 Champions League tactical talking points
Sources.Context: Manchester City, Bayern and Chelsea in the Champions League
Sources.Observation: Bayern used one wide player to provide delivery and the opposite side to attack the box. City used central connections to open the far side.

Sources.Title: In Possession, Out of Possession: FM’s tactical evolution
Sources.Observation: FM represents the two phases as separate shapes and roles. The same player can occupy different locations across those phases.

Sources.Title: The watchmaker behind the Clockwork Oranje
Sources.Observation: Wingers and overlapping full-backs stretched the pitch while Johan Cruyff moved to find openings. Position changes depended on movement, fitness and understanding.

Sources.Title: FC Barcelona commemorates Johan Cruyff’s legacy
Sources.Context: Barcelona’s Dream Team and four consecutive league titles
Sources.Observation: Barcelona describes Cruyff’s coaching model in terms of keeping the ball, finding space and creating numerical superiority.

Sources.Title: Coach profile: Arrigo Sacchi
Sources.Observation: Sacchi’s high line and zonal 4-4-2 required coordinated pressure and movements across the whole team.

Sources.Title: 2008/09 Champions League technical report
Sources.Observation: United combined screening midfielders, overlapping full-backs and quick counters from different starting depths.

Sources.Title: 2006/07 Champions League technical report
Sources.Observation: Arsenal used a holding player in midfield and quick transitions. The team could move between 4-4-2 and 4-5-1.

Sources.Title: Inter’s effective pressing against Atlético de Madrid
Sources.Context: Champions League round of 16, first leg
Sources.Observation: Atlético alternated an advanced block with a compact mid-block and chose when to apply pressure.

Rules.Title: Cover behind the attack
Rules.Detail: Checks the central defenders, a holding player and the cover left when a full-back or wing-back advances.

Rules.Title: Width and wide support
Rules.Detail: Checks both flanks and gives extra importance to the weaker outlet. Wide slots, winger roles and overlapping players can provide width.

Rules.Title: First press and supporting line
Rules.Detail: Checks the front players and midfield support separately, with extra weight on the weakest recovery defender. The engine can moderate the pressing frequency.

Rules.Title: Midfield screen and compact block
Rules.Detail: Looks for players able to screen central lanes in front of the defensive line.

Rules.Title: Build-up connections
Rules.Detail: Checks the defenders who start moves and the midfielders who receive under pressure. A strong average gives limited reassurance when one link struggles.

Rules.Title: Wing-backs and recovery
Rules.Detail: Tests both wing-backs for delivery, stamina, positioning and recovery to their defensive slots.

Rules.Title: Forward partnership
Rules.Detail: Checks whether the pair offers both a player to link attacks and a runner who can stretch the back line.

Rules.Title: Counter-attack outlet
Rules.Detail: Checks the threat that stays available in the defensive shape and the supporting players who can supply the first forward pass.

Rules.Title: First ball and second ball
Rules.Detail: Checks that the direct outlet can contest the first pass and that nearby players can collect the second ball.

Rules.Title: Wide delivery and box presence
Rules.Detail: Pairs the quality of wide service with movement and aerial presence in the box.

Adjustments.Text: More Often. Keep the high press and use more selective pressing triggers.
Standard. Use a safe outlet when the central build-up is under pressure.
Low Crosses. Look for cutbacks when the XI lacks a strong aerial target.
